short: A company's profit for ordinary shareholders divided by the number of its shares, showing how much profit each share has earned.
kid: Your class bakes one big cake and cuts it into 20 equal slices. If the cake gets bigger, every slice gets bigger too. If you cut it into more slices, each slice gets smaller.
detail: Earnings per share (EPS) is net profit attributable to equity shareholders, after any preference dividends, divided by the weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding during the period. Basic EPS uses shares actually in issue; diluted EPS also counts shares that could be created from stock options, warrants and convertible securities, so it is never higher than basic EPS. TTM EPS adds up the last four quarters. Indian companies report both basic and diluted EPS under Ind AS 33 in their results. EPS is the 'E' in the price-to-earnings ratio, so analysts' EPS forecasts drive target prices, and stocks often move on whether reported EPS beats or misses estimates. The common confusion: a higher EPS is not automatically better. A buyback can lift EPS without any rise in profit, one-off gains can inflate it, and EPS cannot be compared across companies because share counts differ.
example: Say ABC Ltd earns a net profit of ₹500 crore, pays ₹20 crore of preference dividends and had 40 crore shares outstanding on average. Basic EPS is ₹12 (480 / 40). If employee options could add 8 crore shares, diluted EPS falls to ₹10 (480 / 48).
formula: EPS = (Net profit - Preference dividends) / Weighted average shares outstanding

short: The highest and lowest prices a stock or index has traded at over the past year, a quick gauge of where today's price sits.
kid: You check the price of your favourite ice cream every day for a whole year. The most it ever cost and the least it ever cost tell you if today's price is high or low.
detail: The 52-week high is the highest price at which a security traded over the previous 52 weeks; the 52-week low is the lowest. Together they form the 52-week range. Most data providers, including NSE and BSE, use intraday prices rather than closing prices, and adjust past prices for splits and bonus issues. Exchanges and financial websites publish daily lists of stocks hitting new 52-week highs and lows, which traders read as signs of momentum and market breadth: many stocks making new highs suggests a broad rally, many making new lows suggests stress. Some momentum strategies favour stocks trading near their 52-week high. The common confusion: a stock at its 52-week low is not automatically cheap, and one at its high is not automatically expensive. Price alone says nothing about value; compare it with earnings and cash flows, and find out why the price moved.
example: Say ABC Ltd traded between ₹420 and ₹780 over the past year and now trades at ₹740. It is about 5.1% below its 52-week high ((780 - 740) / 780) and about 76% above its 52-week low ((740 - 420) / 420).
formula: Distance from 52-week high = (52-week high - Current price) / 52-week high x 100

short: The highest price or level a stock, index or other asset has ever reached in its trading history.
kid: The tallest tower of blocks you have ever built is your best ever. When today's tower goes higher than that, you have a brand new record.
detail: An all-time high (ATH) is the highest level a stock, index, commodity or currency has ever traded at, after adjusting past prices for splits, bonus issues and similar corporate actions. Indian newspapers often say 'lifetime high' or 'record high' for the same idea. A headline about the Sensex or Nifty 50 hitting a fresh high usually means the index has crossed its previous intraday or closing peak. Highs matter because almost everyone who ever bought is sitting on a gain at that price, so there is little selling from holders waiting to break even, and momentum traders often buy such breakouts. The common confusions: an all-time high does not mean a stock is overvalued, since earnings may have grown even faster, and nominal highs ignore inflation. Remember too that recovering a fall needs a bigger percentage gain than the fall itself.
example: Say an index peaks at 10,000 and then falls 20% to 8,000. To get back to its all-time high it must rise 25%, since 8,000 x 1.25 = 10,000.

short: A group of companies that earn money from similar products or services, such as banking, IT services, pharmaceuticals or cement.
kid: In a toy shop, all the dolls sit on one shelf, all the cars on another and all the puzzles on a third. Each shelf holds things that are alike.
detail: A sector is a broad grouping of companies whose main business is similar, used to organise markets, indices, research and portfolios. Global systems include GICS, created by MSCI and S&P Dow Jones Indices, which has 11 sectors broken down into industry groups, industries and sub-industries, and ICB from FTSE Russell. In India, NSE classifies listed companies in a four-level structure running from macro-economic sector down to basic industry, and publishes sectoral indices such as Nifty Bank, Nifty IT and Nifty FMCG. Sectors matter because companies in one sector share drivers, such as interest rates for banks or the dollar for IT exporters, so investors compare valuations within a sector and track sector weights to control risk. The common confusion: 'sector' and 'industry' are often used as synonyms, but in formal systems an industry is a narrower slice of a sector, and conglomerates span several sectors.
example: Say your ₹10 lakh portfolio holds ₹4 lakh in two private banks and ₹2 lakh in a non-bank lender. All three sit in the financial services sector, so 60% of your money ((4 + 2) / 10) depends on the same set of drivers.

short: Moving investment money out of some industries and into others as the economy, interest rates or investor mood change.
kid: In summer the lemonade stand is busy, and in winter the hot cocoa stand is busy. A clever kid moves her helpers to whichever stand is about to get busier.
detail: Sector rotation is the shift of money from one group of industries to another, either as a deliberate strategy or as a description of market flows. The textbook version follows the business cycle: financials and consumer discretionary often lead in early recovery, industrials and technology in mid-cycle, energy and materials late in the cycle, and defensives such as consumer staples, healthcare and utilities when growth slows. Interest rates, commodity prices, government spending and earnings revisions also drive rotations. Indian market reports often describe money moving, for example, from IT services to banks or from consumer stocks to capital goods. Rotation matters because it can lift an index while many stocks fall, and fund managers' sector bets explain much of their performance against benchmarks. The common confusion: the cycle map is a tendency, not a rule. Every cycle differs, and timing the turns is hard.
example: Say a ₹500 crore equity fund cuts its IT weight from 20% to 12% and raises banks from 25% to 33%. It sells ₹40 crore of IT stocks (8% of ₹500 crore) and buys ₹40 crore of bank stocks.

short: Shares of a company expected to grow sales and profits much faster than average, so investors often pay a high price for today's profits.
kid: A tiny puppy can cost a lot for its size, because everyone knows it will grow big. People pay today for how big it will be later.
detail: A growth stock belongs to a company whose revenue and earnings are expected to rise faster than the overall market for several years, often because it is gaining share in a fast-expanding market. Such companies usually reinvest most of their profit instead of paying large dividends, and their shares trade at high price-to-earnings or price-to-sales multiples because investors are paying for future profits. Growth investing is the style that seeks these companies, and index providers publish growth indices alongside value indices. Growth stocks tend to be more sensitive to interest rates, because more of their value lies in distant cash flows, which are discounted more heavily when rates rise. The common confusion: a great growth company is not automatically a great growth stock. If the price already assumes years of rapid growth, a small disappointment can cut the multiple and the share price sharply.
example: Say ABC Ltd earns EPS of ₹20 and trades at 60 times earnings, or ₹1,200. If EPS grows 25% a year for three years to about ₹39 but the market's multiple falls to 30, the price would be about ₹1,172, slightly lower despite earnings nearly doubling.

short: Shares that trade cheaply compared with the company's profits, assets or dividends, often because the business is mature or out of favour.
kid: At the end of the fair, a stall sells good teddy bears for half price because nobody noticed them. Picking up a good thing that others are ignoring is a bargain.
detail: A value stock trades at a low price relative to measures of fundamental worth, such as earnings (low P/E), book value (low P/B), cash flow, or dividends (high dividend yield). Such companies are often mature, slower-growing or temporarily unpopular, for example during an industry downturn or after a management problem. Index providers build value indices from these metrics, and in India factor indices such as the Nifty50 Value 20 follow a value approach. Investors buy value stocks expecting the gap to close through a re-rating, steady dividends or recovering profits. Academic studies found that cheap stocks beat expensive ones over many decades, though value lagged badly for much of the 2010s. The common confusion: a low multiple can be a warning, not a bargain. A value trap is a stock that looks cheap because its earnings are about to shrink, so always ask why a stock is cheap before buying.
example: Say ABC Ltd earns EPS of ₹25 and trades at ₹200, a P/E of 8, while its peers trade at 12. If profits hold steady and the market re-rates it to 12 times, the price would reach ₹300, a 50% gain without any earnings growth.

short: Shares of a company whose sales and profits rise strongly when the economy booms and fall sharply when it slows.
kid: An ice cream van is very busy on hot days and very quiet on cold ones. Its good times and quiet times come round again and again, just like the weather.
detail: A cyclical stock is one whose earnings track the economic cycle closely. Demand for its products, such as cars, steel, cement, machinery, homes, chemicals or air travel, rises when incomes and investment grow and drops when they shrink. Many cyclical companies also have high fixed costs, so a small change in sales causes a big swing in profit. In India, autos, metals, real estate and capital goods are typical cyclical sectors, and banks are partly cyclical through loan growth and bad loans. Cyclicals tend to lead in recoveries and fall hardest in downturns. The key confusion is the valuation trap: cyclicals often look cheapest on P/E at the peak, when earnings are temporarily high, and most expensive at the bottom, when earnings are depressed. Analysts therefore value them on normalised or mid-cycle earnings, or on price-to-book.
example: Say ABC Steel earns EPS of ₹50 at the top of the cycle and trades at ₹400, a P/E of 8. In a downturn EPS falls to ₹10 and the price to ₹250, so the P/E jumps to 25 even though the share price has dropped 37.5%.

short: Shares of a company selling everyday essentials, such as food, soap or medicines, whose profits stay fairly steady even when the economy slows.
kid: Even on a rainy day, people still buy bread and toothpaste. A shop that sells things people always need stays busy whatever the weather.
detail: A defensive stock belongs to a company whose demand holds up through the economic cycle because people keep buying its products in good times and bad. Typical defensive sectors are consumer staples (in India, FMCG makers of soaps, foods and toothpaste), pharmaceuticals and healthcare, utilities such as power distribution, and sometimes telecom. Their earnings are steadier and their shares usually have a low beta, meaning they move less than the market. Investors rotate into defensives when they expect a slowdown or when markets are volatile, and out of them in strong recoveries. The common confusion: defensive does not mean safe. Defensive stocks can still fall, especially when bought at high valuations, and Indian FMCG leaders have often traded at rich multiples, so a slowdown in volume growth can hurt their prices. Rising interest rates can also weigh on bond-like defensives such as utilities.
example: Say the broad market falls 20% in a sell-off, and ABC Consumer Ltd has historically moved about 0.6 times as much as the market (a beta of 0.6). A rough expectation is a 12% fall (0.6 x 20%), smaller than the market's but still a loss.

short: A certificate traded on a US exchange in dollars that represents a fixed number of shares of a foreign company held by a bank.
kid: Your cousin far away wants one of your stickers but cannot visit. You keep the sticker safe in a box and send her a ticket that says she owns it.
detail: An American Depositary Receipt (ADR) is a dollar-denominated certificate, issued by a US depositary bank, that represents shares of a non-US company. The underlying shares sit with a custodian in the home market, and each ADR represents a set number of shares, or a fraction of one. ADRs trade on US exchanges or over the counter and pay dividends in dollars, so US investors can own foreign companies without an overseas account. They come in levels: Level I trades over the counter, Level II lists on an exchange, and Level III lists and raises fresh capital. Infosys became the first Indian company to list on a US exchange, through ADRs on Nasdaq in 1999. Arbitrage keeps the ADR price close to the home-market price converted at the exchange rate. The common confusion: an ADR is not a separate class of shares; it is a receipt for ordinary shares held elsewhere.
example: Say each ADR of ABC Ltd represents 2 shares that trade at ₹1,680 in Mumbai. At an assumed ₹84 to the dollar, 2 shares are worth ₹3,360, so the ADR should trade near $40 (3,360 / 84), before fees.
formula: ADR fair price = Home-market share price x Shares per ADR / Exchange rate (home currency per dollar)

short: A certificate, usually listed in London or Luxembourg, that represents shares of a company from another country and is sold to investors worldwide.
kid: You keep your best toy at home, but you hand out picture cards of it to friends in many towns. Each card means its holder owns a little piece of your toy.
detail: A Global Depositary Receipt (GDR) is a negotiable certificate issued by a depositary bank that represents shares of a company and is offered to investors in more than one country outside the company's home market. GDRs are usually denominated in US dollars or euros and listed on exchanges such as the London Stock Exchange or the Luxembourg Stock Exchange. The mechanism mirrors an ADR: the underlying shares are held by a custodian in the home country, and each receipt represents a fixed number of shares. Indian companies used GDRs widely in the 1990s and 2000s to raise foreign capital; under the rules as of 2025, issues are governed by the Depository Receipts Scheme, 2014. The common confusion is between the two receipts: an ADR is aimed at US investors and trades in the US, while a GDR targets international investors and usually trades in Europe. Indian rules spell it 'depository'.
example: Say ABC Ltd, an Indian company, issues 10 million GDRs in London at $20 each, with each GDR representing 4 shares. It raises $200 million, and 40 million new shares (4 crore) are held by a custodian in India on behalf of the GDR holders.

short: A rupee certificate traded on Indian exchanges that represents shares of a foreign company, letting Indian investors own it locally.
kid: A shop in another country keeps its toys there, but hands out tickets here so children in your town can own a little piece of them.
detail: An Indian Depository Receipt (IDR) is a rupee-denominated instrument issued by a domestic depository in India against shares of a company incorporated outside India, with the underlying shares held by an overseas custodian. IDRs list and trade on Indian exchanges like ordinary shares, letting Indian investors own a foreign company without sending money abroad. The framework sits in the Companies Act and SEBI's issue regulations. In practice the market has been tiny: Standard Chartered PLC's 2010 issue, in which 10 IDRs represented one share, is the only IDR ever issued in India, and it was later delisted. Thin trading, tax uncertainty and limits on converting IDRs into the underlying shares kept investor interest low. Today they matter mainly in policy debates on foreign listings. The common confusion: an IDR is the reverse of an ADR, a foreign company coming to India rather than an Indian company going abroad.
example: Say a foreign company's share trades at £8 in London and 10 IDRs represent one share. At an assumed ₹110 to the pound, one share is worth ₹880, so each IDR should trade near ₹88 in India, before costs.
formula: IDR fair price = Overseas share price x Exchange rate / IDRs per share

short: The standard type of share that gives part-ownership of a company, voting rights and a claim on profits after everyone else is paid.
kid: Ten friends each bring a plank to build a treehouse, so each one owns a piece of it. They all get a vote on the rules, and they all share the fun.
detail: Common stock, called equity shares in India and ordinary shares in the UK, is the basic unit of ownership in a company. Holders usually get one vote per share on matters such as electing directors and approving mergers, and they receive dividends when the board declares them, though dividends are never guaranteed. Common shareholders hold the residual claim: in a liquidation they are paid only after creditors and preference shareholders, so they bear the most risk but also capture all the upside if the company grows. Their liability is limited to what they paid for the shares. Most shares traded on the NSE, BSE or NYSE are common stock. The common confusion is with preference shares, which carry a fixed dividend and priority over common shares but usually no voting rights. Some companies also issue shares with differential voting rights, which break the one-share-one-vote rule.
example: Say ABC Ltd has 10 crore equity shares and you own 1 lakh of them, or 0.1% of the company. If the board declares a dividend of ₹5 per share, you receive ₹5 lakh, and you cast 0.1% of the votes at the annual general meeting.

short: The total number of a company's shares currently held by all its shareholders, including promoters, institutions and the public.
kid: A pizza is cut into 8 slices and your friends are holding all 8. If it is cut into more slices instead, each slice is a smaller part of the pizza.
detail: Shares outstanding is the number of a company's issued shares held by investors, including promoters, insiders, institutions and the public. It excludes treasury shares that a company has bought back and still holds; in India, shares bought back must generally be extinguished, so issued and outstanding counts are usually the same. The figure changes when a company issues new shares, buys back shares, or carries out a split or bonus issue. It feeds directly into market capitalisation and per-share measures such as EPS and book value per share, with EPS using the weighted average count over the period. Fully diluted shares add shares that could be created from employee stock options, warrants and convertible securities. The common confusion is with free float, which counts only shares readily available for trading and excludes promoter and other locked-in holdings. Index weights use free float; market capitalisation uses all shares outstanding.
example: Say ABC Ltd has 50 crore shares outstanding and trades at ₹200, so its market capitalisation is ₹10,000 crore. If employee options could add 2 crore shares, its fully diluted share count is 52 crore.
formula: Shares outstanding = Shares issued - Treasury shares

short: The fixed amount written on a share when it is first created, such as ₹1, ₹2 or ₹10, unrelated to its market price.
kid: A sticker has a small number printed on its back when it is made. Later, friends may swap much more or much less for it, but the printed number never changes.
detail: Face value, also called par value or nominal value, is the value per share stated in a company's memorandum of association; in India it is commonly ₹1, ₹2, ₹5 or ₹10. Share capital on the balance sheet equals shares issued times face value, and anything investors paid above face value goes to the securities premium account. Face value has almost nothing to do with market price: a share with a ₹2 face value can trade at ₹2,000. It matters in three places. Indian companies often declare dividends as a percentage of face value; a stock split cuts face value, for example turning one ₹10 share into five ₹2 shares; and the Companies Act, 2013 generally bars issuing shares below face value. The common confusion is reading a '300% dividend' as a huge return: it is 300% of face value, not of the share price.
example: Say ABC Ltd has a face value of ₹2 per share and declares a 150% dividend. Each share receives ₹3 (150% of ₹2). With the share trading at ₹600, that is a dividend yield of just 0.5%.
formula: Share capital = Shares issued x Face value; Dividend per share = Declared dividend % x Face value

short: Judging what a company is really worth by studying its business, finances, management and industry, then comparing that worth with its share price.
kid: Before swapping for a bike, you check that the wheels spin, the brakes work and the chain is not rusty. Then you decide if it is worth what your friend is asking.
detail: Fundamental analysis estimates a security's intrinsic value from the economic facts behind it, then buys when the price is below that value or sells when it is above. For a company, the analyst studies the industry and competition, the business model and its moat, management quality and governance, and the financial statements: revenue growth, margins, return on capital, cash flow and debt. These feed a forecast and a valuation, using a discounted cash flow model or multiples such as P/E and EV/EBITDA compared with peers. Analysts work top-down (economy, then sector, then company) or bottom-up (company first). In India, the raw material comes from annual reports, quarterly results, earnings calls and exchange filings. The common confusions: a good company is not always a good stock, since the price may already reflect its quality, and fundamental analysis differs from technical analysis, which studies price and volume patterns rather than the business.
example: Say ABC Ltd earns ₹100 crore a year and has 10 crore shares, so EPS is ₹10. If comparable companies trade at 20 times earnings, an analyst might put fair value near ₹200 per share; at a market price of ₹150, the stock looks undervalued if those earnings are durable.

short: The work of analysts who study companies and publish forecasts, valuations and buy, hold or sell recommendations on their shares.
kid: Before the school fair, one child visits every stall, tastes the treats and writes a little note about which are the best. Other children read the notes before they choose.
detail: Equity research is the analysis of listed companies to forecast their earnings and value their shares. Sell-side analysts at brokerages and investment banks cover a list of companies, build financial models, meet management, attend earnings calls and publish reports with a rating (buy, hold or sell, or variants such as add and reduce) and a 12-month target price. Their reports go to institutional clients, whose trading commissions or research fees pay for them. Buy-side analysts at mutual funds, insurers and hedge funds do similar work privately for their own portfolio managers. Report types include initiating coverage, results updates, sector notes and thematic pieces. In India, anyone giving research for a fee must register with SEBI under its Research Analysts Regulations, 2014. The common confusions: a target price is an estimate, not a promise, and sell-side ratings lean heavily towards buy, so read the reasoning and numbers rather than the label.
example: Say an analyst forecasts EPS of ₹40 for ABC Ltd next year and believes the stock deserves 25 times earnings. The target price is ₹1,000 (40 x 25); with the stock at ₹800, that implies 25% upside and a buy rating.
formula: Target price = Forecast EPS x Target P/E multiple

short: Buy side: firms that invest money, like mutual funds. Sell side: firms that sell them shares, research and trading services, like brokers and banks.
kid: At a fruit market, some people come with baskets to buy apples, and others stand behind stalls helping them buy. Both are busy, but they do different jobs.
detail: The buy side is made up of institutions that buy securities to invest money for themselves or their clients: mutual funds, insurance companies, pension funds, hedge funds, private equity firms, family offices and sovereign wealth funds. The sell side is made up of firms that create, distribute and trade securities and sell services to those investors: investment banks, brokerages, market makers and their research teams. Sell-side analysts publish research widely; buy-side analysts advise their own fund's portfolio managers and do not publish. Sell-side firms earn fees and commissions, while buy-side firms earn management and performance fees on the money they run. Many careers start on the sell side and later move to the buy side. The common confusions: 'sell side' has nothing to do with being bearish, and in M&A a 'sell-side mandate' means advising the seller of a business, a different use of the phrase.
example: Say a mutual fund (buy side) managing ₹20,000 crore asks a broker (sell side) to buy ₹100 crore of ABC Ltd shares. At an assumed commission of 0.05%, the broker earns ₹5 lakh for executing the order.

short: A call held after a company announces quarterly results, where management explains the numbers and answers questions from analysts and investors.
kid: After sports day, the team captain stands up and explains why the team won or lost, and then the parents ask questions. Everyone leaves knowing a bit more.
detail: An earnings call is a conference call or webcast that a listed company holds shortly after releasing its quarterly or annual results. The CEO and CFO open with prepared remarks on performance, segment trends and strategy, then take questions from analysts and institutional investors; Indian investors often call it a concall. Calls matter because they add context the results table cannot: demand trends, pricing, margins, capital spending plans and any guidance for coming quarters. Share prices often move as much on management's tone and answers as on the reported numbers. Under SEBI's listing rules as of 2025, listed Indian companies must announce calls in advance and post the audio recording and transcript on their websites. The common confusions: guidance is an estimate, not a commitment, and calls open with a safe-harbour statement warning that forward-looking comments may not come true. Notice what management avoids answering, too.
example: Say ABC Ltd's CFO says on the call that the EBITDA margin should rise from 14% to 16% next year. On unchanged revenue of ₹2,000 crore, that implies EBITDA rising from ₹280 crore to ₹320 crore, an increase of about 14%.

short: A country whose economy and stock markets are growing and opening up but are less rich, deep or accessible than developed ones.
kid: Some gardens are big and fully grown, while others are newer and still sprouting fast. The young gardens can grow quickly, but a storm can knock them about more.
detail: An emerging market is an economy moving from lower incomes and limited capital markets towards developed status, typically with faster growth, rising incomes and institutions that are improving but still maturing. For investors the label comes mainly from index providers such as MSCI, FTSE Russell and S&P Dow Jones Indices, which classify each country as developed, emerging or frontier using economic development, market size and liquidity, and how easily foreigners can invest and move money. As of 2025, India is classed as emerging, alongside China, Brazil and South Africa. Classification matters because huge sums in index and benchmarked funds follow these lists, so a weight change or an upgrade can trigger large foreign flows. The common confusions: market access matters as much as income, so some high-income Gulf states are classed as emerging, and providers do not always agree. Frontier markets are smaller and less accessible still.
example: Say a passive emerging-market fund of $10 billion tracks an index in which one country's weight rises from 18% to 20%. The fund must lift its holdings there from $1.8 billion to $2 billion, buying about $200 million of that country's shares.

short: A company whose shares are admitted for trading on a stock exchange, so anyone can buy or sell them through a broker.
kid: Some lemonade stands sell little pieces of themselves at the town market, where anyone can come and buy one. Those stands must tell everyone how they are doing.
detail: A listed company is one whose shares have been admitted to trading on a recognised stock exchange, such as the NSE or BSE in India or the NYSE and Nasdaq in the US, usually after an initial public offering or a direct listing. Listing gives the company access to public capital and gives shareholders liquidity and a daily market price. In return it accepts continuing obligations. In India, SEBI's Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements (LODR) regulations require quarterly results, prompt disclosure of price-sensitive events, independent directors and audit committees, and a minimum public shareholding, set at 25% under the rules as of 2025 with time allowed for new listings. The common confusion in India is between 'public' and 'listed': a public limited company is a legal form that may or may not be listed, and many are not. Only listing lets ordinary investors trade the shares on an exchange.
example: Say ABC Ltd lists 20 crore shares at ₹150 each, giving a market capitalisation of ₹3,000 crore. If promoters hold 70%, the public holds 30%, worth ₹900 crore, which meets a 25% minimum public shareholding rule.

short: Shares of companies that are not traded on any stock exchange, bought and sold privately with no public daily price.
kid: Most toys are sold in the big toy shop where everyone can see the price. Some are swapped quietly between friends, so nobody is quite sure what they are worth.
detail: Unlisted shares are equity shares of companies not listed on a recognised stock exchange: startups, private companies, large firms that have not gone public, and companies preparing for an IPO. In India, trades happen through specialised dealers, wealth platforms or private deals, and the shares move between demat accounts off-market. Investors are drawn by the chance to buy before an IPO, but the risks are real. Prices are quoted by dealers rather than discovered on an exchange, bid-ask spreads are wide, disclosure is thin and exits can be slow. Pre-IPO holdings are also locked in for a period after listing under SEBI's rules as of 2025, and gains are taxed differently from listed shares. The common confusion: a high unlisted-market price does not mean the IPO will be priced higher. Several Indian IPOs have been priced well below earlier unlisted quotes, leaving pre-IPO buyers with losses.
example: Say you buy 500 unlisted shares of ABC Ltd at ₹600 each, paying ₹3 lakh. If the company later sets its IPO price at ₹450, your holding is worth ₹2,25,000 at that price, a 25% loss before the shares even list.

short: A stock index that assumes all dividends paid by its companies are reinvested, so it shows the full return an investor would earn.
kid: Your apple tree grows taller each year, and it also gives you apples. Counting both the growing and the apples shows everything the tree gave you.
detail: A total return index (TRI) tracks a basket of stocks assuming every dividend is reinvested in the index, typically on the day each stock goes ex-dividend. A price return index, the version quoted in the news for the Nifty 50 or Sensex, tracks only price changes and so dips when stocks pay out dividends. Over long periods the gap compounds, so a price index understates what investors actually earned. That is why SEBI required Indian mutual funds to benchmark their schemes against TRI versions of indices from February 2018; comparing a fund that keeps its dividends with a price index flatters the fund. Global providers publish gross and net total return versions, where net deducts withholding tax on dividends. The common confusion: the index level in headlines is almost always the price index, so its long-run return is not the full return of owning the market.
example: Say a price index rises from 1,000 to 1,100 in a year, while its companies pay dividends worth 15 index points, reinvested at year-end. The price return is 10%, but the total return index ends at 1,115, a total return of 11.5%.
formula: Total return = (Ending price - Starting price + Dividends) / Starting price

short: An individual who invests their own savings in shares, mutual funds or bonds, usually in much smaller amounts than professional institutions.
kid: Big shops buy apples by the truckload, but your mum buys a small bag for the family. She is shopping for her own home, not for a shop.
detail: A retail investor is an individual investing personal money through a broker, a mutual fund or an app, as opposed to an institution managing other people's money. In India, retail participation has surged since 2020, with crores of new demat accounts and steady monthly SIP flows into mutual funds, making individuals a much bigger force in the market. SEBI also uses the term in IPOs: a retail individual investor applies for shares worth up to ₹2 lakh and, under the rules as of 2025, gets a reserved portion: at least 35% in book-built IPOs by profitable companies. Retail flows matter because they can cushion markets when foreign investors sell. Regulators guard retail investors closely, since they usually have less information and are prone to herd behaviour, as SEBI's studies of heavy F&O losses showed. The common confusion: 'retail' in 'retail inflation' or 'retail sector' has nothing to do with investors.
example: Say ABC Ltd's ₹1,000 crore IPO reserves 35% for retail investors, or ₹350 crore. If retail bids total ₹3,500 crore, the retail portion is subscribed 10 times, so many applicants get only a minimum lot by lottery, or nothing.

short: An organisation, such as a mutual fund, insurer, pension fund or bank, that invests large pools of money on behalf of others.
kid: Instead of every child buying sweets alone, the whole class puts its pocket money in one big jar, and one grown-up buys sweets for everyone.
detail: An institutional investor is an organisation that pools money from many people, or holds a large balance sheet, and invests it professionally. Examples include mutual funds, insurance companies such as LIC, pension and provident funds, banks, sovereign wealth funds, endowments, hedge funds and private equity firms. Indian market reports split them into domestic institutional investors (DIIs) and foreign portfolio investors (FPIs, still often called FIIs), and exchanges publish their net buying and selling every day. Institutions account for a large share of trading and own much of the free float, so their flows move prices and their votes shape corporate governance decisions. In IPOs, SEBI defines qualified institutional buyers (QIBs), who get a separate portion of the issue. The common confusion: institutions are not a single bloc. Domestic funds often buy when foreign investors sell, and an insurer's long-term goals differ sharply from a hedge fund's.
example: Say a pension fund managing ₹50,000 crore decides to raise its equity allocation from 10% to 12%. It needs to buy ₹1,000 crore of shares (2% of ₹50,000 crore), enough to move prices in smaller stocks.

short: A person with a large amount of money to invest, commonly at least $1 million in investable assets, who gets specialised wealth services.
kid: Most children have a few coins in their piggy bank, but a few have a big jar full to the top. Grown-ups with very full jars get special helpers to look after them.
detail: A high net-worth individual (HNI or HNWI) is a person with substantial wealth available to invest. Global wealth reports usually set the line at $1 million of investable assets, excluding the main home, and ultra-high net-worth individuals (UHNIs) at about $30 million; banks and wealth managers set their own thresholds. In India the term also has a specific market meaning. Under the rules as of 2025, IPO bidders applying for more than ₹2 lakh fall in the non-institutional investor (NII) category, commonly called the HNI portion, which is split into ₹2-10 lakh and above-₹10 lakh segments. HNIs can also access products with high minimum investments, such as portfolio management services and alternative investment funds. Their money drives private banking and can swing IPO demand. The common confusion: 'HNI' in IPO reports describes a bid-size category, not a verified level of wealth.
example: Say an investor bids for 1,000 shares at ₹500 each in an IPO, a ₹5 lakh application. That is above the ₹2 lakh retail limit, so under the rules as of 2025 the bid falls in the non-institutional (HNI) category, in the ₹2-10 lakh segment.

short: A stock that makes up a large share of an index's value, so its price moves have an outsized effect on the index.
kid: On a see-saw, one big child can tip the whole thing even while the small children wriggle. A big stock in an index is like that big child.
detail: An index heavyweight is a constituent with a large weight in an index, so its price changes move the index more than most other members do. Weights in major indices such as the Nifty 50, Sensex and S&P 500 are based on free-float market capitalisation, so the heavyweights are the largest companies by the value of shares available to the public, not those with the highest share price. In India, large private banks, Reliance Industries and leading IT companies have long been among the biggest Nifty 50 weights. Heavyweights matter because a handful of them can push an index up or down even when most stocks move the other way, which is why market reports name them when explaining the day's move. The common confusion: a high share price does not make a stock a heavyweight, and an index rising does not mean most stocks rose.
example: Say a stock makes up 12% of an index at 10,000 and rises 3% while every other member is flat. It adds 0.36 percentage points to the index (12% x 3%), or 36 points, on its own.
formula: Contribution to index change = Stock's index weight x Stock's % change

short: Nickname for seven giant US technology-led companies: Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia, Meta Platforms and Tesla.
kid: Picture seven giants playing in a sandpit with lots of small children. When the giants jump, the whole sandpit shakes.
detail: The Magnificent Seven is a nickname, coined by Bank of America strategist Michael Hartnett in 2023, for Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia, Meta Platforms and Tesla. They became some of the world's largest companies by market value and drove a large share of US stock market gains, helped by enthusiasm about artificial intelligence. Because the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 are weighted by market capitalisation, the group came to make up an unusually large share of those indices, so its earnings and share prices can set the direction of US markets and of global funds benchmarked to them. The label replaced the older FAANG (Facebook, Amazon, Apple, Netflix, Google), while 'Big Tech' is a looser term for the largest technology firms. The common confusions: the seven are not one sector, and their returns have often diverged sharply. Heavy concentration also means an index fund is less diversified than it looks.
example: Say seven stocks make up 30% of an index. If they rise 10% while the other 70% of the index is flat, the index rises 3% (30% x 10%), even though most of its members went nowhere.

short: Indian news shorthand for the total market value of all companies listed on the BSE; its daily change is reported as wealth gained or lost.
kid: Your toy box seems worth more on days when friends really want your toys, and less on days they don't. Nobody took a toy away; only how much friends want them has changed.
detail: Investor wealth is the phrase Indian media use for the combined market capitalisation of all companies listed on the BSE. When the market falls, headlines say investors lost a certain number of lakh crore rupees, and when it rises, they say investors grew richer by that amount. The number is simply the change in total BSE market capitalisation over the day or period. It is a vivid gauge of how big a move was, and the same total is used in market-cap-to-GDP comparisons. The common confusions: the loss is on paper, measured at the latest traded prices, and becomes real only for those who sell. It is not money that has left the market or gone to someone else. It also includes promoter, government and institutional holdings, not just retail investors, and new listings can raise the total without any price gains.
example: Say the total market capitalisation of BSE-listed companies falls 2% in a day, from ₹400 lakh crore to ₹392 lakh crore. Headlines would say investors lost ₹8 lakh crore, although no shares or cash left anyone's account.
formula: Change in investor wealth = Total BSE market capitalisation now - Total BSE market capitalisation earlier

short: Buying assets for less than a careful estimate of what they are really worth, then waiting for the price to catch up.
kid: A toy that should cost 10 coins is on sale for 6 coins. You buy it and wait, because one day people will see it is worth more.
detail: Value investing is the discipline, set out by Benjamin Graham and David Dodd in Security Analysis (1934) and in Graham's The Intelligent Investor (1949), of buying a security only when its price is well below its intrinsic value. The gap is the margin of safety, a cushion against errors in the estimate and against bad luck. Graham's 'Mr Market' parable treats price swings as offers to exploit rather than verdicts to obey. Warren Buffett, Graham's student, shifted the emphasis from statistically cheap stocks towards wonderful businesses bought at fair prices, adding quality, moats and capital allocation to the analysis. Many well-known Indian fund and portfolio managers describe themselves as value investors. The common confusion: value investing is not the same as buying low-P/E stocks. A fast-growing company can be a value investment if its price is below its worth, and a low-P/E stock can be a value trap.
example: Say an analyst estimates ABC Ltd's intrinsic value at ₹1,000 per share and buys only at ₹650 or less. At ₹650 the margin of safety is 35% ((1,000 - 650) / 1,000), so even if the true value were 35% below the estimate, the investor would not have overpaid.
formula: Margin of safety = (Intrinsic value - Price) / Intrinsic value

short: An investing style that looks for companies with strong earnings growth whose shares are not too expensive for that growth.
kid: You want a plant that grows fast, but you do not want to swap all your toys for it. You look for a quick grower at a fair swap.
detail: Growth at a reasonable price (GARP) blends growth and value investing. A GARP investor wants companies with consistent, above-average earnings growth but refuses to pay any price for it, so valuation acts as a filter. The best-known tool is the PEG ratio, the P/E divided by the expected annual earnings growth rate; a PEG around 1 or below is often treated as reasonable. Peter Lynch, who ran Fidelity's Magellan Fund from 1977 to 1990, popularised the approach. GARP investors avoid both expensive hyper-growth stories and cheap but stagnant businesses, so their portfolios tend to be less extreme than pure growth or value ones. The common confusions: the PEG depends entirely on a growth forecast that may be wrong, and it ignores balance-sheet strength, cash conversion and how long growth can last. A low PEG based on a one-year growth spurt is not the same as one based on durable growth.
example: Say ABC Ltd trades at 30 times earnings with expected EPS growth of 30% a year, a PEG of 1.0, while XYZ Ltd trades at 20 times earnings with 10% growth, a PEG of 2.0. A GARP investor would prefer ABC despite its higher P/E.
formula: PEG ratio = P/E ratio / Expected annual EPS growth rate (in %)

short: A short, clear argument for why a particular investment should make money, what the market is missing, and what would prove it wrong.
kid: Before swapping your toy for a friend's, you say out loud why it is a good swap and what would make you change your mind. That little reason is your plan.
detail: An investment thesis is the reasoning behind buying or selling a security, written so that someone else can test it. A good thesis states what the market currently believes and prices in, what you believe differently and why, the evidence behind your view, the catalysts that should bring the market round, the valuation and expected return, the key risks, and the signposts that would show the thesis is broken. Professional investors write one before taking a position and revisit it every quarter. In stock pitches and interviews, the thesis is usually summed up in two or three crisp points. It matters because it separates a decision from a hunch and tells you when to sell: when the thesis plays out or fails, not when the price merely moves. The common confusion: describing a good company is not a thesis; a thesis must explain why the price is wrong.
example: Say ABC Cement trades at ₹300, or 10 times EPS of ₹30. The thesis: a new plant will lift EPS to ₹40 within two years and the market will pay 12 times, giving ₹480, a 60% upside. It is broken if the plant is delayed by more than a year.

short: An event that could make the market change its mind about a stock and move its price, such as results or a deal.
kid: A sleepy cat lies in the sun all afternoon until the food bowl rattles. The rattle is the thing that makes it jump up.
detail: A catalyst is a specific event or development that could close the gap between a stock's price and an analyst's view of its value. Hard catalysts have a known date or a clear outcome: quarterly results, a regulatory approval, a plant starting production, a demerger, a buyback, index inclusion, an open offer or a court ruling. Soft catalysts are gradual: a new management team, improving industry pricing, or a turnaround becoming visible in margins. Macro events such as an RBI policy decision or the Union Budget can act as catalysts for whole sectors. Catalysts matter in theses and stock pitches because being right about value is not enough; without a trigger, an undervalued stock can stay undervalued for years. The common confusion: 'the stock is cheap' is not a catalyst. A good catalyst is identifiable, likely to happen within the investment horizon and big enough to change earnings or sentiment.
example: Say ABC Ltd trades at ₹500, which the analyst thinks reflects only its core business, while its unlisted subsidiary is worth about ₹100 per share. A demerger due next quarter is the catalyst: once the subsidiary lists separately, the two pieces could be worth ₹600 combined, a 20% gain.

short: A short, structured recommendation to buy or sell a stock, laying out the idea, valuation, catalysts and risks to persuade investors.
kid: You try to convince your friends to pick your favourite game at break time. You explain why it is fun, why it beats the others, and what could go wrong.
detail: A stock pitch is a concise argument for going long (buying) or short (selling) a stock, presented to a portfolio manager, investment committee, interviewer or competition panel. A typical structure runs: the recommendation, target price and expected return; a brief company overview; two or three thesis points explaining why the market is mispricing the stock; valuation, often a DCF alongside peer multiples; catalysts and timeline; and key risks, with what would change your mind. Strong pitches show a variant perception backed by evidence and numbers, not just a description of a good business. In interviews and Indian B-school competitions, pitches are judged on clarity, thesis quality and the handling of questions. The common confusion: a long pitch on a great company can still fail if the upside is small or already priced in, and short pitches need extra care because losses on a short position are theoretically unlimited.
example: Say you pitch ABC Ltd as a long at ₹250 with a 12-month target of ₹325, a 30% upside. For a short pitch on XYZ Ltd at ₹400 with a target of ₹300, the expected gain is 25% if the price falls as predicted.
formula: Expected return on a long = (Target price - Current price) / Current price

short: A well-researched view about a stock that differs from what most investors believe, and that the investor expects to be proved right.
kid: Everyone in class says it will rain at the picnic, but you looked at the sky carefully and think it will be sunny. If you are right, you are the one who packed the kite.
detail: Variant perception, a phrase popularised by hedge fund manager Michael Steinhardt, means holding a well-founded view that differs meaningfully from the market consensus. Because the consensus view is already reflected in the price, returns above the market come only from being different and right. Investors first pin down what the market expects, through consensus earnings estimates, implied valuation multiples or a reverse DCF, then show exactly where and why their own forecast differs. It sits at the centre of any strong investment thesis or stock pitch: interviewers and portfolio managers routinely ask what the market does not understand. The common confusions: being contrarian for its own sake is not variant perception, and a different view is worthless unless it is backed by evidence and likely to be recognised by the market, ideally through a catalyst. If your view matches the consensus, even a correct analysis may earn no excess return.
example: Say consensus expects ABC Ltd to earn EPS of ₹50 next year, and at 20 times earnings the stock trades at ₹1,000. Your research on a new contract suggests EPS of ₹60; at the same multiple that is worth ₹1,200, a 20% upside that exists only if your view proves right.

short: When a brokerage analyst publishes a first, in-depth report on a company, setting a rating and target price for its stock.
kid: A new reporter joins the school newspaper and writes a big first story about the football team. After that, she writes a short update after every match.
detail: Initiating coverage is the start of regular research on a company by a sell-side analyst. The initiation report is usually the most detailed piece the analyst will write: an overview of the business and industry, the investment thesis, financial forecasts, valuation, a rating such as buy, hold or sell, a target price and the key risks. After initiation, the analyst follows up with shorter notes on quarterly results and major events. Brokerages initiate when a company becomes large or liquid enough to interest clients, after an IPO once any quiet period ends, or when a new analyst joins. Headlines about a broker initiating coverage with a buy rating can move a stock, especially a smaller one with little coverage. The common confusion: an initiation is an opinion, not new information about the company, and banks that managed a company's IPO often initiate with favourable ratings, so read the reasoning critically.
example: Say a broker initiates coverage on ABC Ltd at ₹720 with a buy rating and a 12-month target price of ₹900. The implied upside is 25% ((900 - 720) / 720).

short: An NSE index of the 150 Indian companies ranked 101st to 250th by total market value, the standard benchmark for midcap stocks.
kid: Line up all the children in school from tallest to shortest. Skip the 100 tallest, and the next 150 make up the middle group.
detail: The Nifty Midcap 150, run by NSE Indices, tracks the 150 companies ranked 101 to 250 by full market capitalisation within the Nifty 500. Stocks are weighted by free-float market capitalisation, and the index is reviewed twice a year. The ranking mirrors SEBI's mutual fund categorisation under the rules as of 2025: large caps are the top 100 companies, mid caps are 101 to 250 and small caps are 251 onwards, based on lists AMFI publishes every six months. That is why most midcap mutual funds benchmark against the Nifty Midcap 150 TRI. BSE's closest equivalent is the BSE 150 MidCap index. Midcaps tend to grow faster and fall harder than large caps, so the index is watched as a gauge of risk appetite. The common confusion: the Nifty Midcap 100 and Nifty Midcap 50 are different, narrower indices, and a stock's midcap status changes as its market value moves.
example: Say a midcap fund returns 18% in a year while the Nifty Midcap 150 TRI returns 21%. The fund underperformed its benchmark by 3 percentage points, even though 18% looks strong on its own.

short: An NSE index of the 250 Indian companies ranked 251st to 500th by total market value, the standard benchmark for smallcap stocks.
kid: Line up all the children in school from tallest to shortest. Skip the 250 tallest, and the next 250 make up the small group, who are still growing.
detail: The Nifty Smallcap 250, run by NSE Indices, tracks the 250 companies ranked 251 to 500 by full market capitalisation within the Nifty 500, weighted by free-float market capitalisation and reviewed twice a year. It matches SEBI's definition of small caps (companies ranked 251st onwards) for mutual funds under the rules as of 2025, so most smallcap funds benchmark against its TRI. BSE's closest equivalent is the BSE 250 SmallCap index. Small caps can deliver high returns in bull markets but are less liquid, less researched and far more volatile, and the index has suffered drawdowns of 50% or more in past bear phases such as 2008 and 2018-2020. It is watched as a gauge of retail froth. The common confusions: the index covers only ranks 251 to 500, while hundreds of smaller listed companies sit outside it, and index returns can hide much deeper falls in individual small caps.
example: Say ₹1 lakh in a smallcap index fund falls 40% in a bear market to ₹60,000. To get back to ₹1 lakh it then needs a gain of about 67% (40,000 / 60,000), which is why smallcap drawdowns hurt so much.

short: Indian news label for recently listed, technology-led consumer and internet businesses, such as food delivery, fintech and online retail firms.
kid: Some shops are new and live inside phones instead of on the street. They grow very fast, but many are still learning how to make more than they spend.
detail: New-age tech stocks is Indian market shorthand for venture-backed, technology-driven consumer businesses that listed mainly from 2021 onwards, in areas such as food delivery, quick commerce, fintech and payments, online beauty and fashion, insurance marketplaces and logistics. Examples include Zomato (now Eternal), Paytm, Nykaa, PB Fintech (Policybazaar), Delhivery and Swiggy. Many listed while still loss-making, which SEBI's rules as of 2025 allow if at least 75% of the issue goes to institutional buyers, so investors value them on revenue growth, unit economics and the path to profit rather than on P/E. The 2021 listing boom was followed by a sharp sell-off in 2022 as interest rates rose; several fell well below their IPO prices before some recovered strongly. They matter because they show how Indian markets price growth and influence private-market valuations. The common confusion: 'tech' here means consumer internet platforms, not IT services exporters such as Infosys or TCS.
example: Say a new-age company lists at ₹1,000 per share, falls 60% to ₹400 in a tech sell-off and then rebounds 100%. It ends at ₹800, still 20% below its IPO price even after doubling from the bottom.
